title: Why Tech CEOs Are Quietly Cancelling Their AI Plans
description: Tech CEOs spent the last two years promising AI would replace workers, cut costs, and transform everything. Now they're quietly cancelling data centers, rehiring humans and admitting the math doesn't work. From Microsoft pulling back on billions in infrastructure to Starbucks killing its AI inventory system after it couldn't count milk, Uber burning through a year of AI budget in four months, and one company accidentally spending $500 million on AI tools in a single month the AI hype is hitting reality. Even Sam Altman now says he was wrong about AI replacing jobs.
transcript: Tech CEOs spent the last two years promising AI would replace workers, cut costs, and transform everything. Even Sam Altman now says he was wrong about AI replacing jobs.

top_reply.author: @scotttaylor9133
top_reply.text:
For development this is the biggest issue I see, regardless of how embedded or how much you want it to do.  Every subscription, model, etc. is sold on being constantly updated and 'learning from you as it goes to get better'.  That means a lack of  idempotence and thus stability in the process.

Idempotence means that every time you ask for ketchup the same way, you get the same ketchup back (or slightly geekier same input gets you the same output).  This is setup where asking the same way over time gets you different ketchup, meaning that you can't really train the people to use the tool, because it's not constant in how it works.  This also means that you can't reproduce the output over time, and small changes have the potential of introducing large errors in unrelated sections of code to a degree you don't see with surgical changes (because the AI could change anything).  This would require very, VERY tight automated test suites to make this work and actually replace people.  The change in jobs from doing programming to reading massive batches of code looking for slight logical errors is not an easy one.  Code review is hard, and if you have a developer where you're constantly finding serious errors during code review, you generally fire them because you aren't likely to catch everything.  Code review is not equal to QA.

I feel this problem will exist in most fields.  Some fields (like legal review prior to filings) are much more accustomed to this type of work, but for a  field like development this is a very big change in what made people want to do the job and enjoy it initially compared to what the job now is, to the degree that it requires a different personality type (imo).
